narrative:
The 2024 Atlanta Braves were a team defined by stubborn resilience and frustrating fragility in equal measure. They arrived at spring training as defending division champions and World Series contenders, yet the season quickly revealed a roster navigating life without a fully healthy Ronald Acuña Jr. and a bullpen that would prove to be their Achilles' heel. Still, Atlanta's lineup — anchored by Marcell Ozuna's breakout offensive campaign, Austin Riley's steady production, and a catching corps led by Sean Murphy and Travis d'Arnaud — kept them competitive through wave after wave of adversity.

The Braves sprinted out of the gate with a dominant April, posting a 17-8 record that suggested another division title run was imminent. Marcell Ozuna was the story of that early stretch, launching a three-run walk-off blast in mid-April that captured the team's early electricity. But cracks appeared almost immediately in the bullpen. Raisel Iglesias and A.J. Minter both surrendered crushing home runs in April and May, and the team's inability to protect late leads became a recurring nightmare that would define the summer months. May arrived with a .500 record and a growing sense that this would be a fight, not a coronation.

The middle months of the season were a grinding war of attrition. June and July produced near-.500 baseball, with Joe Jiménez serving up back-breaking doubles and Pierce Johnson coughing up leads at the worst possible moments. Yet every time the Braves seemed ready to collapse, they steadied themselves. August brought a winning record thanks in part to opportunistic moments like Michael Harris II reaching on a throwing error to spark a comeback, and Travis d'Arnaud's home run late in September kept their playoff hopes alive. A dramatic Ozzie Albies double on September 30th nearly saved their season in the final weekend, only for Pierce Johnson to surrender a Francisco Lindor two-run shot that encapsulated the bullpen's torment all year long.

Atlanta scratched into the Wild Card round but ran into a San Diego Padres lineup that was peaking at the perfect moment. Max Fried, one of the best pitchers in baseball, was battered across two games as Manny Machado, Jackson Merrill, and others ran roughshod over Atlanta's pitching. Michael Harris II provided a brief spark with a postseason home run, but it was not nearly enough. The Braves were eliminated in the Wild Card round, finishing 89-73 — a winning season by any measure, but one that felt like an opportunity lost given the talent on the roster. The bullpen's failures, which echoed across nearly every chapter of this story, ultimately wrote the ending.

chapters.title: April Explosion
chapters.description: The Braves tear through April with the best record in baseball, led by Ozuna's monster three-run blast and a lineup firing on all cylinders.

chapters.title: Bullpen Cracks Widen
chapters.description: A brutal stretch of late-game meltdowns from Minter, Iglesias, and Jiménez drags Atlanta to .500 as May and June turn treacherous.

chapters.title: Grinding Through Summer
chapters.description: The Braves win ugly through July and August, surviving bullpen disasters with clutch offense and timely errors working in their favor.

chapters.title: September's Last Stand
chapters.description: Atlanta battles to secure a Wild Card spot down the stretch, with d'Arnaud and Albies delivering clutch hits before Johnson's late collapse nearly derails everything.

chapters.title: October Ends Early
chapters.description: The Padres dismantle Max Fried and the Atlanta pitching staff in the Wild Card round, ending the Braves' season before it ever truly began.
